The post Put your old vines to the test appeared first on winemag.
content:
Entries are now open for the third annual NFB Old Vine Report, informed by a blind tasting designed to identify the old-vine wines that perform most convincingly in the glass.

The wines will be tasted by editor Christian Eedes, James Pietersen, CEO of Brice & Burnett, and Francois Rautenbach, a hospitality and wine specialist.

Why enter?

  • Your wine is judged blind, without producer or brand influencing the result.
  • Every entry receives a Winemag 100-point score.
  • The Top 10 receive individual tasting notes.
  • Buyer’s-guide exposure (wine’s ranked by quality relative to price).
  • The report puts your wine alongside other leading examples from South Africa’s heritage vineyards.
  • Best Overall recognition goes to the highest-performing wine in the tasting.

Entry fee: R1,495 per wine, including VAT.

To qualify, wines must be made from grapes grown on Certified Heritage Vineyards: vineyards aged 35 years or more, registered with SAWIS and approved by the Old Vine Project.

Entries close 7 October 2026. No late entries will be accepted.

Enter now.


The NFB Old Vine Report is made possible by NFB Private Wealth Management, established in 1985 – because time is the one advantage no investor can buy back.

Winner benefits

The producer of the wine judged Best Overall wins a FERMTECH SOLUTIONS organic fermentation kit worth approximately R10,000 and shipping services worth R10,000 from Aspiring Couriers.

title: Melvyn Minnaar: Initmate art encounters in Riebeek-Kasteel
summary:
With Swartland acknowledged as the modern classic appellation of the art of wine, it is no surprise that a cute village like Riebeek-Kasteel is a hub for artists of many persuasions. In fact, the visual arts bloom throughout the valley. It may be inspired by the delights of the fine, handcrafted wines at hand, but […]

The post Melvyn Minnaar: Initmate art encounters in Riebeek-Kasteel appeared first on winemag.
content:
With Swartland acknowledged as the modern classic appellation of the art of wine, it is no surprise that a cute village like Riebeek-Kasteel is a hub for artists of many persuasions. In fact, the visual arts bloom throughout the valley. It may be inspired by the delights of the fine, handcrafted wines at hand, but the geography has its own undulating, bright charm.

Then there are the villagers, the people nearby, living in the panoramic country reality.

Over the past decade an annual mini arts festival has been crafted that exemplify and suits harmoniously the community of Riebeek and surroundings: the way they live, work, make art and wine. The romance is real, if the vocation is hands-on and focussed. The tourism appeal is genuine and, yes, great fun.

The special ‘art weekend’ goes by the title of Solo Studios, a delightful headline for a programme in which local artists perform solo by opening their studios for art inspection by visitors. If the ‘solo’ suggests individuality, the reality is that each contributes to a whole lot of arty pleasure over the weekend – powered, no doubt, by the splendid wines from local wineries.

This year, celebrating the tenth anniversary, Solo Studios X has enhanced the draw. It takes place over the weekend of October 23 – 25 and the programme is jam-packed (a premier weekend pass is R450 plus booking fee per person).

The organisers are boasting with more than 60 artists, five galleries taking part with numerous exhibitions, walkabouts, talks and workshops. Gardens have temporary installed sculptures to admire. And something unique to experience this year is a special garden.

Over the years, the artistic endeavours have held up a tradition of variety, engagement and ingenuity – with a strong local root. At the same time, over the years, artists from elsewhere have found the friendly environment of the weekend inviting to participate and show up.

Sophisticated paintings and sculpture sit easily next to works produced in community spirit. This is art for joy.

Ashley Stone, one of the organisers, summed it up. “It is about creating moments of connection – between people and place, artists and audiences, creativity and conversation. There is indeed something special about experiencing art in the Riebeek Valley.”

As a regular in recent years, I can confirm that special upbeat feeling. (And we always seem to have boxes of Marras and Riebeek Valley wines in the boot for the return route.)       

What I like about the project is the local collaboration and professionalism – no highbrow attitude in operation here. Sharing the spirit is a solid foundation for this successful project.

How playful, for example, to join Antoinette du Plessis for a ‘blue and white’ ceramic plate painting workshop? Or make your own print under supervision of well-known artist Judy Woodborne. She hosts a printmaking workshop on dry point etching.

Just talking to artists in their studios, viewing their process, is both educational and enriching – much like a glass of, say, Marras Chenin Blanc.

Every year a new twist surprises, and this year it’s a ‘Garden of Edible Delights’ on offer by the Valley Potager. Designed and created by Jan Seidel in the style of a European vegetable and fruit kitchen garden in the centre of the valley, visitors are invited along its paths to see, smell and admire.

The star of the upcoming event is unusual and special: a commemorative limited edition box set of ten original prints by local artists who have participated since the first Solo Studios event ten years ago. 10 Years, 10 Artists, 10 Boxes were compiled as both as artwork and archive of the festival’s milestone year, destined to be a collector’s item. It will be available for sale during the festival.

No doubt this year’s Solo Studios in one of my favourite villages, together with some of my favourite wines will once again send weekend visitors home with – if not an artwork or two, that fine portfolio of prints and cases of local wines – cheerful memories of a very cultured community.

  • Melvyn Minnaar has written about art and wine for various local and international publications over the years. The creativity that underpins these subjects is an enduring personal passion. He has served on a few “cultural committees”.

title: Recipe: Cape Malay chicken curry
summary:
Serve with basmati rice and sambals. Yield This recipe serves 4 people. Cape Malay chicken curry recipe ingredients 1 tbsp (15ml) olive oil 1 onion, finely chopped 1 clove of garlic, crushed 1 chilli, deseeded and finely chopped 2 tbsp (30ml) fresh ginger, finely chopped 2 tsp (10ml) coriander 2 tsp (10ml) cumin 1 tsp […]

The post Recipe: Cape Malay chicken curry appeared first on winemag.
content:
Serve with basmati rice and sambals.

Yield

This recipe serves 4 people.

Cape Malay chicken curry recipe ingredients

  • 1 tbsp (15ml) olive oil
  • 1 onion, finely chopped
  • 1 clove of garlic, crushed
  • 1 chilli, deseeded and finely chopped
  • 2 tbsp (30ml) fresh ginger, finely chopped
  • 2 tsp (10ml) coriander
  • 2 tsp (10ml) cumin
  • 1 tsp (5ml) turmeric
  • 1 tbsp (15ml) garam masala
  • 1 x 400g tin tomatoes
  • ½ cup (125ml) chicken stock or water
  • 600g chicken pieces
  • ½ cup (125ml) coconut milk or plain yoghurt
  • 2 tbsp (30ml) chutney
  • salt and freshly ground black pepper
    squeeze of lemon juice
    10g fresh coriander, chopped

Cooking method

  1. Heat oil in a pot and sauté onion, garlic, chilli and ginger for about 2 minutes. Add coriander, cumin, turmeric and garam masala and fry for further few minutes to release their flavours. Add tomatoes and stock and bring to a simmer.
  2. Add chicken and cook, covered, for 20-30 minutes, or until cooked through. Stir in the coconut milk and chutney. Season with salt and pepper and a squeeze of lemon juice.
  3. Serve curry with basmati rice and sambals. Garnish with freshly chopped coriander.

Wine pairing

This dish will work well with a white wine that has some residual sugar, a more full bodied Chenin Blanc an ideal match. Dare we say it, an IPA from your favourite craft brewer will also do the job.

title: Editorial: The great wine glass con
summary:
One of the great con jobs of wine is the expensive wine glass. We have spent decades being told that the glass is not merely a vessel but an instrument, that its shape directs aromas, concentrates flavours, softens tannins and somehow elevates the whole drinking experience to something rapturous. To be fair, good glassware does […]

The post Editorial: The great wine glass con appeared first on winemag.
content:
One of the great con jobs of wine is the expensive wine glass. We have spent decades being told that the glass is not merely a vessel but an instrument, that its shape directs aromas, concentrates flavours, softens tannins and somehow elevates the whole drinking experience to something rapturous.

To be fair, good glassware does make wine taste better. The problem is that it does not make it that much better.

Consider the South African prices. A pair of Riedel Veloce Cabernet/Merlot glasses available from merchant Reciprocal is R1,345. A two-piece Gabriel-Glas Gold Gift Set from Brice & Burnett is R1,750. A pair of Zalto Balance glasses from Great Domaines will set you back R2,190. At these prices, the wine is no longer necessarily the expensive bit.

The economics of fragility

There is something wonderfully peculiar about the economics. Wine is a consumable: you drink it and buy more. The glass, by contrast, is supposed to be durable. Yet the premium end of the market has engineered these objects to the absolute precipice of structural integrity – making a durable household asset into a slow-burn consumable not because it wears out, but because it is terrifyingly fragile.

This is where the extended cost of ownership enters the picture. First, you buy the glasses. Then you spend the rest of your life worrying about them. You buy the hardware once, but you pay a lifetime subscription fee in pure, unadulterated anxiety. Or, as is unfortunately the case in Chez Eedes, you just keep having to buy new hardware…

The seriousness game

Then, there is the second great trick: ceremony. A wine glass does not merely hold wine. At a certain price point it starts telling others how seriously you take wine. There is a correct bowl, a correct stem, a correct way to hold it, a correct angle at which to examine the colour and, presumably, an incorrect way of drinking something that is ultimately the fermented juice of grapes.

The danger is that the glass becomes part of wine’s unfortunate tendency to turn pleasure into performance. Wine is already burdened with enough ceremony. We have appellations, vintages, viticulture, oenology, typicity and the person at the table who says “there’s a mineral note” before anyone has actually taken a sip. Do we really need a glass that makes wine appreciation feel like a screening process?

The irony is that a good glass is genuinely useful. A generous bowl gives volatile compounds somewhere to go. A narrower rim allows the liquid to hit your tongue just right. Thin glass feels nicer against the lips. Shape affects how wine arrives on the palate. These are not imaginary benefits. But there is a difference between better and transformative.

A R200 glass can be good. A R500 glass can be very good. A R1,000 glass can be lovely. The leap from “lovely” to “this has fundamentally changed my understanding of Pinot Noir” is where I become suspicious.

And what, culturally, are these prices actually connected to? In South Africa, R1,345 is a meaningful amount of money. R2,190 is more than many people would spend on a bottle of wine, let alone the apparatus through which they intend to drink it. The price therefore does not simply represent glassmaking skill. It represents aspiration, design, scarcity, brand mythology and the idea that serious wine requires serious equipment.

Wine has a curious habit of taking a perfectly reasonable proposition – a better glass can improve the experience – and extending it until the proposition becomes you need this particular glass to experience wine properly.

Use good glasses. By all means. If you enjoy the feel of them, the look of them, the ritual of them, spend the money. Pleasure is not required to pass a cost-benefit analysis. But let us stop pretending that a R1,095 glass delivers five times the pleasure of a R219 glass simply because it costs five times as much.

title: Tim James: Why do we drink? And why do I?
summary:
We all drink alcohol, it’s surely fair to say (unless there are some teetotal voyeurs – liseurs? – readingthis; “we” being the readers, extended to “people generally”). But why? That’s my first question, andit’s easier to answer, strangely enough, in the first person plural: why do we (human beings) drinkalcohol, than it is in the […]

The post Tim James: Why do we drink? And why do I? appeared first on winemag.
content:
We all drink alcohol, it’s surely fair to say (unless there are some teetotal voyeurs – liseurs? – reading
this; “we” being the readers, extended to “people generally”). But why? That’s my first question, and
it’s easier to answer, strangely enough, in the first person plural: why do we (human beings) drink
alcohol, than it is in the first person singular: why do I (this particular human being) drink alcohol?

The harder, messier bit I shall return to later. As to why people drink alcohol (to the despair of many,
including the World Health Organisation, which says it’s an unsafe practice at any level of
consumption) – well, I’m convinced by the answers summarised and articulated by Canadian
philosopher Edward Slingerland in his 2021 book called Drunk (subtitled How we sipped, danced, and
stumbled our way to civilization).

I’ve just re-read the book, which I reviewed mostly favourably back in 2023 – have a look there if you
didn’t see it and would like to know more of Slingerland’s arguments and marshalling of the evidence.
Basically, he confronts two facts: first, the overwhelmingly widespread use of alcohol (ahead of a
range of other intoxicants) throughout human history; and, second, the often appalling effects of
alcohol abuse in at least modern society, abuse that’s both social and individual. Given the latter, why
did human evolution allow for and even encourage the former? Why have many governmental
attempts to prohibit its usage seemed doomed to fail?

Because, Slingerland argues (with recourse to everything from pre-history to the structure of the brain
– the need to “dial down the prefrontal cortex”), intoxicants have been crucial to the development of
humans as creative, cultural and communal animals – as well as providing us with comfort and
pleasure.

That’s a very brief summary of his conclusions. As I wrote in my original review, I was convinced by
this argument, and also accepted his uncompromising description of the “dark side of Dionysis” that
seems to have emerged comparatively recently in human history.

Given this evolutionary usefulness, why are there a few societies that don’t have recourse to alcohol,
cannabis, peyote buttons and other hallucinogens and psychedelics? (It seems to have been only
North America where there was historically no use of nature’s escapist and bonding bounty.) This
needs local investigation, which usually reveals other social equivalents – religious ecstasy and
bonding and the like (Trump’s MAGA rallies, perhaps, it occurs to me, in puritanical America).

Fair enough, and that leaves only the question about individual participation or avoidance in drinking.
We here probably know more imbibers than total abstainers, but I’m sure we know some of those.
And we know in some cases that they they are there because they have been badly damaged by
over-indulgence (another recent re-read of mine has been A A Gill’s splendid autobiographical book
Pour Me, which rather entertainingly details the hell of his addiction before he went straight). And we
know in some cases of the substitutes people have. Many people don’t even seem to manage to be
miserable bastards without the occasional drink.

In fact, one of the most excoriated categories of alcohol consumer these days is the solitary drinker –
unaffected, as Slingerland argues, by the subtle social controls generally exercised by communal
consumption, on a large level as still lingers on in cultures like those of the European Mediteranean
countries, or the dining table or pub everywhere. Google the category and you find any number of
warnings, and the images show a lot of the truly miserable, lonely bastards (mostly men) huddled
over their glass or bottle.

I myself do a significant proportion of my wine-drinking solo, almost inevitably around my evening
meal. Worse, these days it usually includes a bit of brandy – and the advent of distillation, giving
unprecedentedly alcohol drinks, is something Slingerland (and no doubt many others) gives some
blame to regarding modern society’s alcohol problems. So perhaps the obvious answer to the
question of why I drink is simply that I’m an old drunk (in the company of the larger part of the wine
industry, in my experience – where usually it’s communal rather than solitary wine-drinking that
obtains, sometimes to the point of leaving me aghast – and comparatively sober).

It doesn’t feel like being simply an old drunk from the inside, and I haven’t had to deal with many
accusations. I seldom get obviously drunk, I’d say, either with others or alone, but admittedly
sometimes there’s more of a buzz than at others, and I certainly enjoy a degree of the buzz. I have
also frequently found that I’m more creative when the buzz is on. I tend to then write a bit more
loosely and uninhibitedly and thoughts flow more interestingly, to the writing’s benefit – though I have
learnt that it’s wise to check my spelling and syntax the next morning. But that’s not a reason, more an
occasional side-benefit. Good wine is pretty delicious and interesting once you’ve got the taste for it,
of course, and that is obviously part of the reason. But probably not all that much more seriously so
than the great world of tea, for example, though more extensive and various.

In the old days of my comparative youth, when I heard of someone’s disease of whatever kind
demanding the total cessation of alcohol consumption I would shudder with horror at the very idea.
Strangely, perhaps, now I think I could cope without alcohol – though I would most certainly not do so
willingly. It seems such an important part of my mealtime, whether a simple or more complex wine
and/or meal. Could I imagine doing as – still, apparently – many American adults and children do, and
have milk or “soda” with my meal? I think not. Or just water? (The aforementioned AA Gill managed,
after all, to be a serious restaurant critic after renouncing alcohol.) Beer, though, can be great,
including my beloved no-alc version Devils Peak Hero. Which reminds me, no also to no-alc wine until
it improves a whole lot (see Jamie Goode’s current piece). Wine, proper wine, retains its supreme
place, even – or arguably especially – for the solitary diner.

  • Tim James is one of South Africa’s leading wine commentators, contributing to various local and international wine publications. His book Wines of the New South Africa – Tradition and Revolution appeared in 2013.

title: Jamie Goode: Zero-alcohol wine has a problem – it doesn’t taste like wine
summary:
A few years back (2009) I was enlisted by a wine company specializing in lower alcohol wines, for me to give them some market support. As someone with a technical background, but also a consumer-focused newspaper column, I was potentially useful to them. The owner was a Brit based in California who had worked with […]

The post Jamie Goode: Zero-alcohol wine has a problem – it doesn’t taste like wine appeared first on winemag.
content:
A few years back (2009) I was enlisted by a wine company specializing in lower alcohol wines, for me to give them some market support. As someone with a technical background, but also a consumer-focused newspaper column, I was potentially useful to them. The owner was a Brit based in California who had worked with the spinning cone, a high-tech way of removing alcohol from wine. He was interesting to work with, although he did have an alarming habit of losing his temper in meetings and slamming his forearm down on the table with more force than was strictly necessary.

I liked the idea. It wasn’t zero-alcohol wine, but wines at perhaps 8% or 5% alcohol, with the proper flavour of wine but less booziness. And with the spinning cone column, they were well placed to make these wines, and benefit from others who saw a market opportunity here.

So after some activity in the UK, I flew to their headquarters in California, where I saw the spinning cone in action, and tasted some of their products. Particularly informative was a tasting where we looked at the same wine at different alcohol levels.

The idea was to start with a wine such as a Chardonnay at 14% alcohol. You take 10 000 litres, which you put through the spinning cone, taking off first the volatile fraction (‘essence’) and then the alcohol, leaving you with 8 250 litres of Chardonnay at 4% alcohol. You then add the aromatic ‘essence’ back in, and the resulting 4% wine can be used as a blending component to add to untreated wine, to result in a final wine at a lower alcohol level.

How did the wines taste? I started off looking at a Californian Chardonnay at 14.3% alcohol. It had a sweet, ripe, slightly buttery nose, leading to a rich buttery palate that was quite broad. I then tasted the same wine after it had been through the spinning cone column, at 4% alcohol. This was more minerally with tangerine notes and some spicy richness. The palate was lemony and tart with hollow fruit and an enhanced sensation of acidity. Their winemaker told me that alcohol is a masking agent so taking it away reveals what’s there. It also adds sweetness to the palate. Also, the acidity is concentrated, and appears higher up in the mix. I guess what this showed is that it really matters what you start off with, when you start taking alcohol out. But also that it has a huge effect on flavour.

The next wine was a blend of 10% of the 4% sample with the remainder of the original wine, resulting in a Chardonnay at 13.2%. This was fresher than the original with more acidity apparent. The fruit showed through more. There was quite a difference, and the 13.2% wine was much nicer than the 14.3% original.

I then tried four different Californian wines each at three alcohol levels: the original level, and then reduced levels of 11% and 8%. A Chardonnay that tasted sweet and buttery at 14% alcohol tasted fresher with nice definition at 11%, and then more lemony and refreshing at 8%. A rosé showed best at 12.2%, and was perhaps less successful at 8%. A Shiraz was sweet, juicy and spicy at 14.6%, but fresher and more vivid with less sweetness at 11%; at 8% it was more savoury with fresh, pure fruit and a more gastronomic character. A Merlot showed really well at 11% and fresh, juicy and bracing with more apparent acidity at 8%. These are inexpensive wines, but with this alcohol reduction they really showed very well.

What was immediately apparent was the role that alcohol has in shaping the flavour and aroma of the wine. Take just a little out, and you have a different wine. But in the region of 8% alcohol and above, you can make some very interesting wines, depending on your starting wine.

But my experience of zero alcohol wine has been quite different. Remove it all, and you have something that really doesn’t taste all that wine like at all. This is for three reasons. First, the alcohol itself is contributing something important to the flavour. It adds some sweetness and richness, and quite a lot of the body. And second, alcohol is acting as a masking agent. We like wines the way they taste, but without alcohol and its masking, suddenly you reveal all sorts of aromas that you didn’t see before. And it smells and tastes different, and a bit weird.

It’s not possible to neatly take off all the aroma compounds in one fraction, then take off the alcohol in a second, and then combine back the aroma compounds. This is because many of the desirable aroma compounds leave in the alcohol stream. The evidence in the scientific literature shows that many of the interesting aroma compounds are lost in the dealcoholization process.

Also, there are significant changes in acidity. For example, one study showed that a white wine where the original level was 6.88 g/L rose to 10.05 g/L in the dealcoholized wine and pH lowers with this from 3.00 to 2.70). This is taking these parameters out of the normal range for table wines.

With much more work on technology, it may be possible to preserve more of the aroma molecules in the wine than is currently possible. But this won’t overcome the second, larger problem faced by non-alcoholic wines – the importance of the non-volatile matrix on aroma release.

But for now, it seems that eliminating alcohol changes so much in a wine that it’s very hard to end up with anything that tastes like wine. For most zero-alcohol wines, it’s normal to add sugar at a level of around 40 g/litre, and the resulting wine doesn’t taste sweet, largely because of the sky-high acidity. But this sort of ultraprocessed wine is sort of at odds with where we are heading in terms of gastronomy at the moment.

I remain optimistic about wines that have just a little alcohol reduced, though. Going from 15% to 12% might be a good thing, or going from 13% to 10%, especially for more commercial styles. Sometimes, picking earlier does this job without intervention. But I’m open to some intervention if the results are good.

  • Jamie Goode is a London-based wine writer, lecturer, wine judge and book author. With a PhD in plant biology, he worked as a science editor, before starting wineanorak.com, one of the world’s most popular wine websites.

The post Put your old vines to the test – time’s running out appeared first on winemag.
content:
Entries are now open for the third annual NFB Old Vine Report, informed by a blind tasting designed to identify the old-vine wines that perform most convincingly in the glass.

The wines will be tasted by editor Christian Eedes, James Pietersen, CEO of Brice & Burnett, and Francois Rautenbach, a hospitality and wine specialist.

Why enter?

  • Your wine is judged blind, without producer or brand influencing the result.
  • Every entry receives a Winemag 100-point score.
  • The Top 10 receive individual tasting notes.
  • Buyer’s-guide exposure (wine’s ranked by quality relative to price).
  • The report puts your wine alongside other leading examples from South Africa’s heritage vineyards.
  • Best Overall recognition goes to the highest-performing wine in the tasting.

Entry fee: R1,495 per wine, including VAT.

To qualify, wines must be made from grapes grown on Certified Heritage Vineyards: vineyards aged 35 years or more, registered with SAWIS and approved by the Old Vine Project.

Entries close 7 October 2026. No late entries will be accepted.

Enter now.


The NFB Old Vine Report is made possible by NFB Private Wealth Management, established in 1985 – because time is the one advantage no investor can buy back.

Winner benefits

The producer of the wine judged Best Overall wins a FERMTECH SOLUTIONS organic fermentation kit worth approximately R10,000 and shipping services worth R10,000 from Aspiring Couriers.

title: Melvyn Minnaar: Initmate art encounters in Riebeek-Kasteel
summary:
With Swartland acknowledged as the modern classic appellation of the art of wine, it is no surprise that a cute village like Riebeek-Kasteel is a hub for artists of many persuasions. In fact, the visual arts bloom throughout the valley. It may be inspired by the delights of the fine, handcrafted wines at hand, but […]

The post Melvyn Minnaar: Initmate art encounters in Riebeek-Kasteel appeared first on winemag.
content:
With Swartland acknowledged as the modern classic appellation of the art of wine, it is no surprise that a cute village like Riebeek-Kasteel is a hub for artists of many persuasions. In fact, the visual arts bloom throughout the valley. It may be inspired by the delights of the fine, handcrafted wines at hand, but the geography has its own undulating, bright charm.

Then there are the villagers, the people nearby, living in the panoramic country reality.

Over the past decade an annual mini arts festival has been crafted that exemplify and suits harmoniously the community of Riebeek and surroundings: the way they live, work, make art and wine. The romance is real, if the vocation is hands-on and focussed. The tourism appeal is genuine and, yes, great fun.

The special ‘art weekend’ goes by the title of Solo Studios, a delightful headline for a programme in which local artists perform solo by opening their studios for art inspection by visitors. If the ‘solo’ suggests individuality, the reality is that each contributes to a whole lot of arty pleasure over the weekend – powered, no doubt, by the splendid wines from local wineries.

This year, celebrating the tenth anniversary, Solo Studios X has enhanced the draw. It takes place over the weekend of October 23 – 25 and the programme is jam-packed (a premier weekend pass is R450 plus booking fee per person).

The organisers are boasting with more than 60 artists, five galleries taking part with numerous exhibitions, walkabouts, talks and workshops. Gardens have temporary installed sculptures to admire. And something unique to experience this year is a special garden.

Over the years, the artistic endeavours have held up a tradition of variety, engagement and ingenuity – with a strong local root. At the same time, over the years, artists from elsewhere have found the friendly environment of the weekend inviting to participate and show up.

Sophisticated paintings and sculpture sit easily next to works produced in community spirit. This is art for joy.

Ashley Stone, one of the organisers, summed it up. “It is about creating moments of connection – between people and place, artists and audiences, creativity and conversation. There is indeed something special about experiencing art in the Riebeek Valley.”

As a regular in recent years, I can confirm that special upbeat feeling. (And we always seem to have boxes of Marras and Riebeek Valley wines in the boot for the return route.)       

What I like about the project is the local collaboration and professionalism – no highbrow attitude in operation here. Sharing the spirit is a solid foundation for this successful project.

How playful, for example, to join Antoinette du Plessis for a ‘blue and white’ ceramic plate painting workshop? Or make your own print under supervision of well-known artist Judy Woodborne. She hosts a printmaking workshop on dry point etching.

Just talking to artists in their studios, viewing their process, is both educational and enriching – much like a glass of, say, Marras Chenin Blanc.

Every year a new twist surprises, and this year it’s a ‘Garden of Edible Delights’ on offer by the Valley Potager. Designed and created by Jan Seidel in the style of a European vegetable and fruit kitchen garden in the centre of the valley, visitors are invited along its paths to see, smell and admire.

The star of the upcoming event is unusual and special: a commemorative limited edition box set of ten original prints by local artists who have participated since the first Solo Studios event ten years ago. 10 Years, 10 Artists, 10 Boxes were compiled as both as artwork and archive of the festival’s milestone year, destined to be a collector’s item. It will be available for sale during the festival.

No doubt this year’s Solo Studios in one of my favourite villages, together with some of my favourite wines will once again send weekend visitors home with – if not an artwork or two, that fine portfolio of prints and cases of local wines – cheerful memories of a very cultured community.

  • Melvyn Minnaar has written about art and wine for various local and international publications over the years. The creativity that underpins these subjects is an enduring personal passion. He has served on a few “cultural committees”.

summary:

The post Recipe: Cape Malay chicken curry appeared first on winemag.
content:
Serve with basmati rice and sambals.

Yield

This recipe serves 4 people.

Cape Malay chicken curry recipe ingredients

  • 1 tbsp (15ml) olive oil
  • 1 onion, finely chopped
  • 1 clove of garlic, crushed
  • 1 chilli, deseeded and finely chopped
  • 2 tbsp (30ml) fresh ginger, finely chopped
  • 2 tsp (10ml) coriander
  • 2 tsp (10ml) cumin
  • 1 tsp (5ml) turmeric
  • 1 tbsp (15ml) garam masala
  • 1 x 400g tin tomatoes
  • ½ cup (125ml) chicken stock or water
  • 600g chicken pieces
  • ½ cup (125ml) coconut milk or plain yoghurt
  • 2 tbsp (30ml) chutney
  • salt and freshly ground black pepper
    squeeze of lemon juice
    10g fresh coriander, chopped

Cooking method

  1. Heat oil in a pot and sauté onion, garlic, chilli and ginger for about 2 minutes. Add coriander, cumin, turmeric and garam masala and fry for further few minutes to release their flavours. Add tomatoes and stock and bring to a simmer.
  2. Add chicken and cook, covered, for 20-30 minutes, or until cooked through. Stir in the coconut milk and chutney. Season with salt and pepper and a squeeze of lemon juice.
  3. Serve curry with basmati rice and sambals. Garnish with freshly chopped coriander.

Wine pairing

This dish will work well with a white wine that has some residual sugar, a more full bodied Chenin Blanc an ideal match. Dare we say it, an IPA from your favourite craft brewer will also do the job.
